title: Engineered Molecular Clock Transitions for Precision Measurements
summary: Special clock transitions in heavy polar molecules have been engineered to probe physics beyond the standard model, suppressing disruptive electromagnetic noise by orders of magnitude while preserving high sensitivity.

title: Charge transport capacity as a probe of resonances in models of many-body localization
summary: Many-body localization (MBL) breaks the standard paradigm of quantum thermalization and has evaded a complete understanding due to mysterious finite-size effects in numerics. Here, by introducing and calculating the charge transport capacity in MBL systems, the authors connect these finite-sized effects to increasingly probable larger many-body resonances with increasing system sizes, occurring even at very strong disorder. A perturbative model explains the physics of these resonances and reconciles these resonances with the possibility of asymptotically stable MBL.

Here, the authors demonstrate how measuring correlations between two qubits, both coupled to the same quantum many-body system, can uncover crucial information about the system itself. These correlations reveal how excitations and fluctuations propagate through space and time, distinguish ballistic from diffusive transport, and provide a sensitive probe of how far the system is driven from equilibrium.

title: Strain engineering of transient exciton diffusion in ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ monolayers at cryogenic temperatures
summary: Here, the authors show how strain allows control of the spatiotemporal exciton dynamics in WSe monolayers at cryogenic temperatures. They demonstrate that tensile strain abruptly increases the excess energy of hot excitons, thereby accelerating their transient diffusion. The authors trace this back to suppressed phonon-mediated scattering from bright to dark excitons. Furthermore, a periodic modulation of the transient exciton diffusion is predicted in the presence of a compressive strain resulting from emission of phonons.
